name: Forehead contouring (bone burring)

card.summary: Surgery that shaves down or reshapes a prominent brow ridge and frontal bone to flatten the forehead and soften the upper face, best known from facial feminization surgery.
card.note: Surgical procedure near the frontal sinus; done by a surgeon under anesthesia.

quick.overview:
Forehead contouring with bone burring reduces a prominent brow ridge by shaving the frontal bone, flattening and smoothing the forehead. It is most commonly performed as part of facial feminization surgery, where the forehead is one of the main visual differences between male and female faces.

For appearance, a smaller brow ridge opens the eye area and changes how masculine or feminine the upper face reads. A 2023 review notes that the upper third of the face strongly affects gender assessment and that forehead contouring is well tolerated with minimal side effects reported.
quick.how: Surgeons shave the bone as far as is safe, sometimes rebuilding surrounding areas with bone cement, or reshape the glabellar bone in a cranioplasty and fix it with plates or wires. It is planned individually, sometimes with 3D imaging and printed guides.
quick.risks: Burring can break through the thin wall of the frontal sinus in people with thin bone. Cranioplasty risks include improper healing, bone fragment movement and cysts, usually correctable with another procedure. Sinonasal symptoms after surgery have been studied in long-term follow-up.

lead: Forehead contouring by bone burring is a surgical technique that shaves down the frontal bone and brow ridge to flatten the forehead. It is a component of facial feminization surgery, pioneered by surgeon Douglas Ousterhout after a 1982 request from a colleague to operate on a trans woman [1].

Its value for appearance is visual: forehead shape is one of the main differences between male and female faces, and upper-face surgery has a large effect on how gender is perceived [1][2]. Techniques include forehead reduction or augmentation, orbital contouring and hairline adjustment [2].

Conservative burring shaves bone without breaking the sinus wall and may add hydroxyapatite cement to the surroundings; cranioplasty detaches, thins and repositions the glabellar bone with plates or wires [1]. Evidence consists of surgical reviews and follow-up studies [2][3].

chain: Prominent frontal bone is shaved or reshaped
angle.text: Surgery changes the bone contour itself. It is used for brow ridge reduction in facial feminization.

paras: Burring: the brow ridge is usually solid bone and can be sanded down, whereas bone above the frontal sinus has a thin wall that can break through. Surgeons burr conservatively and may fill adjacent areas with hydroxyapatite cement [1].

Cranioplasty: the glabellar bone is detached, thinned, reshaped and reattached with titanium wires, plates and screws [1]. Virtual surgical planning and 3D printing are used in facial feminization planning [4].
Douglas Ousterhout developed these procedures in the 1980s drawing on craniofacial reconstruction experience and skull measurements [1].

Reported risks include sinus wall breakthrough, bone-fragment movement and cysts [1]. Long-term follow-up has examined sinonasal symptoms after frontal bone cranioplasty [5]. Pitfalls and complications of facial gender-affirming surgery are reviewed in the surgical literature [6].
Evidence comprises surgical reviews and follow-up studies rather than randomized trials [2][5][6]. Wikipedia notes that data on which approach is better is limited [1].

timeline.event: Surgeon Darrell Pratt asks Douglas Ousterhout to operate on a trans woman, beginning his facial feminization work [1].
